why.extend: Online content ranges from reliable to deliberately deceptive, and generative AI makes convincing fakes cheap to produce. Recognising how language, tone and design signal reliability, and checking claims before acting on them, protects your money and your judgement.

articles.title: The trust test

body.support:
Anyone can post anything online. Some is true. Some is a trick. Here's a quick test.

**1. Who made it?** Is there a real name or website?

**2. Why?** To tell you something? To sell you something? To get your money?

**3. When?** Look for a date. Old stories get shared again.

**4. How does it sound?** Watch out for:

- **urgent** words: *act now!*
- **secrets**: *the trick banks hide*
- **promises**: *guaranteed money*
- **famous faces** “saying” they love it.

**5. Check somewhere else.** Open a new tab. Does a **reliable** site say the same? Search with the photo too.

**Deepfakes.** AI can make fake videos of real people. Lips might not match the words. But fakes are getting better. So use the test.

**Decide:** trust it, check more, or skip it. Report scams to **Scamwatch**.
body.core:
Online, anyone can post anything. Some of it is true. Some is a mistake. And some is built to trick you. Here's a quick test you can run on any post, ad, video or website.

**1. Who made it?** Look for a real name, organisation or website. Click the profile, the “About” page or the web address. No name? Brand-new account? Be careful.

**2. Why was it made?** To inform you? To entertain you? To sell you something? Or to get your money or details? If someone gains from you believing it, check harder.

**3. When was it made?** Old stories and photos often get shared again as if they're new. Look for a date.

**4. How does it sound?** The language and **tone** are clues. Watch out for:

- **urgent** words: *act now, only today, before it's banned*
- **secret** claims: *the trick banks don't want you to know*
- **guarantees**: *guaranteed profits, no risk*
- **fake endorsements**: a famous person “recommending” a product.

Real companies and governments usually sound calm and give details.

**5. Check it somewhere else.** Open a new tab. Do **reliable** sources, like a government site, a trusted news outlet or an expert organisation, say the same thing? For photos, try a **reverse image search** to see where else the image appears.

**Deepfakes.** AI can now make **deepfakes**: fake videos or voices of real people. Signs include lips that don't match the words, strange blinking, blurry edges, odd hands, or a voice that sounds flat. But fakes are getting better, so don't rely on spotting glitches. Rely on the trust test.

**Your verdict.** After the test, decide: **trust it**, **check it more**, or **skip it**. And if it's a scam, report it to **Scamwatch**.
body.extend:
Online content ranges from reliable reporting to honest error to deliberate deception. A short, repeatable test helps you judge any post, ad, video or website.

**1. Who made it?** Identify a real author, organisation or site. Check profiles, “About” pages and web addresses. Anonymous or newly created accounts warrant caution.

**2. Why was it made?** Consider the purpose: to inform, entertain, sell or extract money or data. Where the creator benefits from your belief, scrutinise more closely.

**3. When was it made?** Recycled stories and images often circulate as if new. Check dates.

**4. Language and tone.** Deceptive content often uses **urgency** (*act now*), **secrecy** (*what the banks won't tell you*), **guarantees** (*risk-free returns*) and **false endorsements** from celebrities. Legitimate organisations generally use measured, specific language.

**5. Corroborate.** Check whether **reliable** independent sources (government, reputable news, expert bodies) confirm the claim. Use **reverse image search** to trace an image's origins.

**Deepfakes.** Generative AI can fabricate convincing video and audio of real people. Visual glitches (mismatched lip movement, unnatural blinking, distorted hands) may appear, but fakes are improving, so process matters more than spotting errors.

**Verdict.** Decide to **trust**, **investigate further**, or **disregard**, and report scams to **Scamwatch**.

caseStudies.title: The billionaire who never said it

body.support:
**Andrew Forrest** is one of Australia's richest people.

Scammers used his face in **fake ads** on Facebook and Instagram. The ads said he loved get-rich-quick schemes. Some used **deepfake** videos. He never said any of it. People lost money.

Forrest took **Meta**, the company that owns Facebook and Instagram, to court in the United States. He said Meta should be responsible for the scam ads.

In **June 2024**, a US judge said the case could go ahead.

The lesson: a famous face in an ad doesn't mean they really said it. Check it. If it promises easy money, skip it.
body.core:
**Andrew Forrest**, known as “Twiggy”, is one of Australia's richest people. He made his money in mining.

For years, scammers used his name and face in **fake ads** on Facebook and Instagram. The ads made it look like he was recommending get-rich-quick schemes, often involving cryptocurrency. Some used fake news stories and **deepfake** video. He never endorsed any of them. But people who believed the ads lost money.

Forrest decided to fight back. He sued **Meta**, the company that owns Facebook and Instagram, in a court in **California** in the United States. He argued that Meta should be responsible for the scam ads it ran and made money from.

Meta argued that, under US law, it wasn't responsible for ads made by other people. But in **June 2024**, a US judge disagreed enough to let the case go ahead. The judge said Forrest could try to prove that Meta's own ad tools had helped create the ads.

The lesson for everyone scrolling: a famous face in an ad doesn't mean that person really said it. Check the source. Check the claim. And if it promises easy money, skip it.
body.extend:
**Andrew Forrest**, the mining billionaire known as “Twiggy”, became one of the most-used faces in Australian scam advertising.

For years, fake ads on Facebook and Instagram used his name and image. Some used made-up news stories and **deepfake** video. They pushed get-rich-quick schemes, often using cryptocurrency. He endorsed none of them. But people who trusted the ads lost money.

Forrest sued **Meta**, owner of Facebook and Instagram, in a federal court in **California**. He argued that Meta should be accountable for scam ads it ran and profited from.

Meta argued that US law protected it from blame for ads that other people created. In **June 2024**, a US judge let the case go ahead. The judge found that Forrest could try to show that Meta's own ad tools helped create the ads.

The case shows the limits of trusting your feed. A familiar face is not an endorsement. What makes content reliable is its source, its purpose and checks from elsewhere, not how polished it looks.

teacher.overview: Students learn a five-step trust test for online content (who made it, why, when, how it sounds, and what other reliable sources say), including warning signs in language and tone (urgency, secrecy, guarantees, fake endorsements), reverse image searching, and deepfakes. They annotate a made-up scam ad, sort content into trust it, check it or skip it, and trust test a real piece of content, explaining their verdict to a group. The case study is Andrew Forrest's lawsuit against Meta over scam ads using his face and name, which a US judge allowed to proceed in June 2024.
prep: Collect a few safe examples of real content to model (screenshots, not live links to scams).
Show how to do a reverse image search on school devices.
Remind students not to tap links in suspicious content.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** who made it, why, when, how it sounds, check elsewhere. E.g. urgent words, secret claims, guarantees, fake endorsements. Fakes are getting better, so glitches may not show; the test still works.

**Scam ad:** 1 new account pretending to be news; 2 secret claim in capitals; 3 possible deepfake; 4 guarantee with no risk; 5 urgency; 6 fake comments from new accounts.

**Sort:** BoM warning — trust; celebrity crypto — skip; influencer supplements — check; screenshot headline — check; guaranteed returns — skip; Services Australia page — trust.

**Case study:** famous faces borrow trust; answers will vary on responsibility; check the person's official channels, search the claim, check news coverage and Scamwatch.
